![](resources/sampling-frames-introduction-hero.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

Sampling frames form the geographical and statistical foundation of censuses and household surveys. They provide the structure for comprehensive census enumeration and the basis for selecting primary sampling units and, subsequently, households or individuals for surveys. Their quality directly affects the representativeness of survey samples and the reliability of estimates of population characteristics, such as health, economic circumstances and public perceptions. Maintaining reliable frames is nevertheless challenging. Rapid population growth, urban expansion and forced displacement can make existing frames obsolete, while political sensitivities may restrict access to official census materials. Frames may also be geographically incomplete where armed conflict, insecurity or limited resources prevent enumeration in parts of a country.

Automated approaches can help overcome these constraints by generating bespoke sampling units from alternative geospatial data. Compared with conventional frame construction, automation can make the process faster, more reproducible and easier to apply consistently across large or heterogeneous study areas. It can also facilitate more frequent updates where settlement patterns or population distributions are changing rapidly. These methods are therefore especially useful where standard sampling frames are unavailable, outdated or poorly aligned with the requirements of a particular survey. 

The automated generation of reliable sampling frames remains an unresolved challenge, and although several approaches have been proposed, no single solution is suitable for all survey and census contexts. Recent developments led by researchers at Real Good Research include gridEZ ([Dooley 2025](https://cadooley.github.io/gridEZ_tutorials/); [Dooley et al. 2025](https://github.com/cadooley/gridEZ)), which uses gridded population estimates to generate gridded enumeration zones that meet a user-defined population target and can serve as primary sampling units for household surveys. Its relatively simple approach enables large frames to be generated quickly and requires only widely available gridded population estimates as input data. These advantages have supported the increasing use of gridded survey designs, accompanied by the development of fieldwork procedures for sampling units whose boundaries do not necessarily correspond to visible features on the ground. Nevertheless, these designs may require additional field-team training and can create challenges in locating boundaries and recording data accurately. Grid-based frames are therefore unsuitable for census enumeration, as grid boundaries may divide individual buildings or require time-consumer routes to cover and do not provide clearly defined units within which all buildings and households can be systematically identified and enumerated. In response to these limitations and enabled by the increasing availability and accuracy of building-footprint data, alternative approaches based on the spatial distribution of buildings are now being developed. One such approach is clusterComposer ([Dooley et al. 2026](https://github.com/cadooley/clusterComposer)), which uses building footprints or building locations with associated population estimates to group buildings into spatially defined sampling units. By generating clusters with well-defined polygon boundaries and populations close to a specified target, clusterComposer is intended to support both bespoke survey-frame generation and the updating of census frames. 
Together, these approaches demonstrate how gridded population and building-level data can support the automated construction or updating of spatial sampling frames. However, their reliability remains dependent on the coverage and accuracy of the underlying population and settlement data. Gaps or inaccuracies in these data may compromise the quality of the resulting sampling frames, potentially leaving some populations unrepresented or affecting their likelihood of selection in surveys. Generating reliable sampling frames therefore requires both better population estimates and robust automated methods. By advancing these areas together, we aim to make accurate sampling frames easier and faster to construct and update, particularly where conventional census-based frames are unavailable, outdated or unsuitable.

Two approaches to automated sampling-frame generation are gridEZ and clusterComposer. The gridEZ algorithm uses gridded population estimates to generate gridded enumeration zones that can serve as primary sampling units for household surveys. In contrast, clusterComposer uses building footprints or building locations with associated population estimates to group buildings into spatially defined sampling units. It generates clusters with well-defined polygon boundaries that approximate a specified target population, supporting the creation of bespoke survey frames and the updating of existing census frames. Together, these approaches demonstrate how gridded population and building-level data can support the automated construction or updating of spatial sampling frames where conventional census-based frames are unavailable or unsuitable.
